skill.name: Connect two texts: what one adds to the other
skill.why: One text rarely tells the whole story. A second text can fill the gaps.
skill.how: Read both. Ask what Text B tells you that Text A didn't.

steps.say: Two texts can team up. Ask: what's new in Text B?

creature.name: Bridgle
creature.blurb: A sugar glider that leaps between two gum trees, carrying what one tree has to the other. Link two texts and it glides further.

write.ask: Write one sentence that says what Text B adds to Text A.
given: Text A (a poster): The school pool opens on Monday.
Text B (Zed's message, Sunday night): The pool won't open until Wednesday. The heater broke.
checks: I said something only Text B tells you.
I didn't repeat what both texts say.
I named the job, like reason, update or correction.
write.model: Text B is an update: the pool now opens on Wednesday, because the heater broke.

encounters.frame: Wren is studying platypuses. The Bridgle is carrying facts between her book and her notes.
encounters.text: Text A (an encyclopedia entry): The platypus is a small, shy animal found in rivers and creeks in eastern Australia. It has a flat bill like a duck's, webbed feet and thick brown fur. Platypuses dive underwater to hunt for food, with their eyes, ears and nostrils shut. Instead, they find food by sensing tiny electric signals from the bodies of worms, shrimp and insect larvae. Males have a sharp spur on each back leg that can deliver a painful venom. Text B (Wren's survey notes): Spent the whole evening at Stringybark Creek. Saw two platypuses just after sunset, diving again and again near the fallen log to find food. Each dive lasted about thirty seconds. One came up chewing so hard that I could hear it. Gravel in its cheeks helps it grind up food, because adults have no teeth. Counted fifty-six dives in an hour. Did not see the sharp spurs that males have on their back legs, so they may both have been females.
encounters.prompt: Where does each fact come from? Match each one to the right tree.
encounters.success: Some facts are in both, even when Wren only shows them, like the spurs she uses to guess.

encounters.frame: A rocket launch has been held up. The Bridgle found two reports about it.
encounters.text: Text A (a notice from Hollowgum Space Centre): The launch of the Kestrel 2 rocket has been delayed. It will now take off on Thursday at 6 am, three days later than planned. Kestrel 2 will carry a small weather satellite into orbit, where it will help scientists track storms over the Southern Ocean. Visitors with tickets for Monday's launch can use them on Thursday instead. Text B (an engineer's blog): Here's what really held us up. On Sunday morning, we found that a pair of seagulls had built a nest on the launch tower, right beside the rocket. There were two speckled eggs in it. We can't launch with birds that close, and moving an active nest is against the rules. So we called a wildlife expert, who said the eggs were about to hatch. We decided to wait. The chicks hatched on Tuesday, and the whole family has now moved to a quieter roof. Our weather satellite is still safe and ready to go.
encounters.prompt: What does Text B add to Text A?

encounters.text: Text A (from the diary of Ada Cole, aged twelve, the lighthouse keeper's daughter, 9 June 1902): A terrible storm last night. At about two o'clock, Father woke me, shouting that a ship was on the rocks below Hollowgum Point. We could see her lamps swinging wildly in the dark. It was the schooner Curlew, carrying timber to the mainland. Father and two fishermen rowed out three times in the little lifeboat, and by dawn they had brought all eleven sailors safely ashore. I made tea until my arms ached. The Curlew broke apart before breakfast, and planks are still washing up along the beach. Text B (a plaque at the Hollowgum Maritime Museum): The Wreck of the Curlew. In 1902, the timber schooner Curlew struck the rocks off Hollowgum Point during a winter storm. For more than a century, nobody knew exactly where her remains lay. Then, in 2019, two local divers searching for crayfish spotted a ship's bell half buried in the sand. The bell was cleaned and found to carry the name Curlew. Divers have since mapped the wreck, which lies fourteen metres underwater and is now home to schools of fish and a large, grumpy groper.

encounters.text: Text A (from a doctor's handbook printed in 1840): For a patient suffering from fever, headache or a general weakness of the body, the application of leeches is strongly advised. The illness is caused by an excess of bad blood, which must be drawn out if the patient is to recover. Place six to twelve leeches upon the skin of the temples or chest and allow them to feed until they fall away of their own accord. Leeches may be kept alive in a jar of pond water and used again. So the team placed medical leeches on the finger. Leech saliva contains a chemical that stops blood from clotting, which keeps it flowing while new veins grow. Doctors stressed that the old idea of draining bad blood to cure fevers was wrong, and that each leech is used only once.

I couldn't stop thinking about it. So I've propped my easel by the kitchen fire, and I'm painting the storm from his description. I've put Tom's boat in the corner, so he'll never forget how lucky he was.
